verses.zh: 祸哉！那些设立不义之律例的和记录奸诈之判语的，
verses.en: Beware, those who enact unjust policies[NOTE:1] those who are always instituting unfair regulations,[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Woe [to] those who decree evil decrees.”
Heb “[to] the writers who write out harm.” The participle and verb are in the Piel, suggesting repetitive action.
verses.commentary:
10:1 "Woe" This INTERJECTION (BDB 222) is used often in Isaiah (and Jeremiah).
It is translated (NASB 1995 Update)

- "alas," Isa. 1:4; 17:12

- "ah," Isa. 1:24

- "woe," Isa. 5:8,11,18,20,21,22; 10:1,5; 18:1; 28:1; 29:1,5; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1; 45:9,10; 55:1
(i.e. woe oracles)

- "ho," Isa. 55:1; also possibly Isa. 10:5

It denotes anguish and pain or a summons (i.e. #4 above). There is another
INTERJECTION (BDB 17), which is usually translated "woe," which expresses
grief and despair (cf. Isa. 3:9,11; 6:5; 24:16 and 8 times in Jeremiah).

▣ The parallelism of Isa. 10:1a and b links the civil leaders (i.e. those who enact evil
statutes) and judges (who constantly record unjust decisions, cf. Isa. 5:23). Israel's leadership has
knowingly violated the Mosaic covenant emphasis on care for the poor, socially ostracized, and socially
powerless people (cf. Isa. 10:2; 1:17,23; 3:14,15; 11:4; Deut. 16:19; 24:17; 27:19; Prov. 17:23; 18:5;
Amos 4:1; 5:12).

▣ "statutes" See SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION

verses.zh: 为要屈枉穷乏人，夺去我民中困苦人的理，以寡妇当作掳物，以孤儿当作掠物。
verses.en: to keep the poor from getting fair treatmentand to deprive[NOTE:1] the oppressed among my people of justice,so they can steal what widows ownand loot what belongs to orphans.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “rob” (ASV, NASB, NCV, NRSV); KJV “take away the right from the poor.”
On the socio-economic background of vv. 1-2, see the note at 1:23.tn Heb “so that widows are their plunder, and they can loot orphans.”
verses.commentary:
10:2 Things are so upside down when the very ones YHWH seeks to protect (i.e. widows and orphans)
have become the spoil and plunder!

verses.zh: 到降罚的日子，有灾祸从远方临到，那时，你们怎样行呢？你们向谁逃奔求救呢？你们的荣耀（或译：财宝）存留何处呢？
verses.en: What will you do on judgment day,[NOTE:1] when destruction arrives from a distant place?To whom will you run for help?Where will you leave your wealth?
notes: Heb “the day of visitation” (so KJV, ASV), that is, the day when God arrives to execute justice on the oppressors.
verses.commentary:
10:3

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB, JPSOA
"day of punishment"

LXX
"day of visitation"

REB
"when called to account"

Peshitta
"day of recompense"

The MT has "day of visitation." This visitation (BDB 924) by YHWH can be for blessing
(i.e. Job 10:12) or punishment. Here, for judgment (cf. Jer. 8:12; 10:15; 49:8; HOs. 9:7; Mic. 7:4).

A series of questions spells out the fate of these exploiters! One day, whether temporally
or eschatologically, the Creator will call His creatures, made in His image and likeness, to give an account
of the stewardship of the gift of life (cf. Isa. 10:4). YHWH is a moral, ethical, compassionate Deity and
He demands these characteristics in His covenant people so that "the nations" may know and come to Him!!
Israel was giving a false message!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "And in the devastation which will come from afar" The judgment visitation by Israel's
covenant God comes at His initiation (cf. Isa. 5:26-30). This is surely a prelude to the exile of Israel by
Assyria and a foreshadowing of the exile of Judah by Neo-Babylon (v. 11).

YHWH's people clearly forgot that His promises were conditional on obedience.
Rebellion has terrible consequences (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

verses.zh: 他们只得屈身在被掳的人以下，仆倒在被杀的人以下。虽然如此，耶和华的怒气还未转消；他的手仍伸不缩。
verses.en: You will have no place to go, except to kneel with the prisonersor to fall among those who have been killed.[NOTE:1] Despite all this, his anger does not subside,and his hand is ready to strike again.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “except one kneels in the place of the prisoner, and in the place of the slain [who] fall.” On the force of בִּלְתִּי (bilti, “except”) and its logical connection to what precedes, see BDB 116 s.v. בֵלֶת. On the force of תַּחַת (takhat, “in the place of”) here, see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:258, n. 6.
Heb “in all this his anger was not turned, and still his hand was outstretched”; KJV, ASV, NRSV “his hand is stretched out still.”sn See the note at 9:12.
verses.commentary:
10:4 "His anger does not turn away" This is the Hebrew root (BDB 996, KB 1427) for repentance.
YHWH's judgment of His faithless covenant people will not turn away (Qal PERFECT).

This very anger on Israel was clearly demonstrated in God's judgment on Jerusalem and
the temple in A.D. 70 by the Roman army (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: SECOND COMING, IV). I have come to believe that

- Matthew 21-25

- Mark 13 (Olivet Discourse)

- Luke 17; 21 (Olivet Discourse)

- 2 Thessalonians 2 ("man of lawlessness")

- the book of Revelation (i.e. Rev. 1:7)

refers to this A.D. 70 event. The new Jewish church is separated completely
from the synagogue. See my exegetical notes on these NT passages free online.

▣ "His hand is still stretched out" This is a recurrent phrase in this literary unit (cf.
Isa. 9:12,17,21). It is an anthropomorphic way of expressing God's unrelenting judgment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE USED TO DESCRIBE DEITY

verses.zh: 亚述是我怒气的棍，手中拿我恼恨的杖。
verses.en: “Beware, Assyria, the club I use to vent my anger,[NOTE:1] a cudgel with which I angrily punish.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Woe [to] Assyria, the club of my anger.”

Heb “a cudgel is he, in their hand is my anger.” It seems likely that the final mem (ם) on בְיָדָם (beyadam) is not a pronominal suffix (“in their hand”), but an enclitic mem. If so, one can translate literally, “a cudgel is he in the hand of my anger.”
verses.commentary:
10:5-19 This is a literary unit on YHWH's activity involving the nation of Assyria. It was the cruelest
ANE power. It was brutal toward captive people groups. YHWH will use this godless pagan nation to
accomplish His purposes (cf. Isa. 10:5b; 6b; as Hab. 1:12-17 asked God about His use of the Babylonian exile).
God uses evil to do His biding! He did not make them (i.e. Satan, demons, fallen angels, evil empires),
but He directs them for the larger good (cf. Job 12:23; Ps.47:7-8; 66:7; Dan. 2:21; Acts 17:26, i.e. His
universal redemptive plan, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN).

However, evil reaps the consequences of their acts. One day they, too, will be judged (cf.
Deut. 32:34-43; Isa. 14:24-27; 30:27-33; 31:5-9). What Assyria did to others, Babylon (cf. Isa. 13:5) will
do to them!

10:5-6 Notice the parallel words for YHWH's using Assyria as the rod of His discipline and judgment towards
His covenant people (v. 6a).

- "My anger," v. 5a, BDB 60 I, cf. Isa. 5:25; 9:12,17,21; 10:4,25; 13:9,13

- "My indignation," v. 5b, BDB 276; cf. Isa. 5:5,25; 13:5; 30:27

- "My fury," v. 6b, BDB 720; cf. Isa. 9:18; 10:6; Jer. 7:29

Covenant love spurned turns into Divine wrath (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28). To whom much is given,
much is required (i.e. Romans 9).

10:5 "Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger" YHWH's tool for punishing His people's rebellion was the
cruel nation of Assyria (cf. Isa. 7:17; 8:7). However, Assyria was responsible for her acts (cf. Isa. 10:24-27).
The arrogance of Assyria is seen in Isa. 10:8-11,12.

verses.zh: 我要打发他攻击亵渎的国民，吩咐他攻击我所恼怒的百姓，抢财为掳物，夺货为掠物，将他们践踏，像街上的泥土一样。
verses.en: I sent him[NOTE:1] against a godless[NOTE:2] nation,I ordered him to attack the people with whom I was angry,[NOTE:3] to take plunder and to carry away loot,to trample them down[NOTE:4] like dirt in the streets.
notes: Throughout this section singular forms are used to refer to Assyria; perhaps the king of Assyria is in view (see v. 12).
Or “defiled”; cf. ASV “profane”; NAB “impious”; NCV “separated from God.”
Heb “and against the people of my anger I ordered him.”
Heb “to make it [i.e., the people] a trampled place.”
verses.commentary:
10:6 "a godless nation. . .the people of my fury" Oh, my, this refers to the nation of Israel (cf.
Isa. 9:17,19)! This same phrase is used of Israel in Isa. 19:17; 32:6. What irony, the covenant people
are called "godless" and said to be morally equivalent to "godless" Assyria!

▣ "To capture booty and to seize plunder" As Isa. 10:21, "a remnant will return," reflects
Isaiah's first son's name (cf. Isa. 7:3), this reflects his second son's symbolic name (cf. Isa. 8:1,3).

verses.zh: 然而，他不是这样的意思；他心也不这样打算。他心里倒想毁灭，剪除不少的国。
verses.en: But he does not agree with this;his mind does not reason this way,[NOTE:1] for his goal is to destroyand to eliminate many nations.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “but he, not so does he intend, and his heart, not so does it think.”
Heb “for to destroy [is] in his heart, and to cut off nations, not a few.”
verses.commentary:
10:7 "Yet it does not so intend

Nor does it plan so in its heart" Assyria did not know that YHWH was directing its actions for
His purposes. Assyria was only after more and more spoil.

The intent of YHWH for the king of Assyria is revealed in a series
of Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS (Isa. 10:6) against Israel.

- capture booty (BDB 1021, KB 1531)

- seize plunder (BDB 102, KB 117)

- trample down (VERBAL BDB 962, KB 1321, NOUN
BDB 942)

The intent of the King of Assyria is expressed in two Hiphil
INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS in Isa. 10:7c,d.

- to destroy (BDB 1029, KB 1552)

- to cut off (BDB 503, KB 500)

verses.zh: 他说：我的臣仆岂不都是王吗？
verses.en: Indeed,[NOTE:1] he says:‘Are not my officials all kings?
notes: Or “For” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV).
verses.commentary:
10:8-11 The King of Assyria's thoughts (i.e. "boasts," TEV) are revealed in these verses.

- all his military commanders are kings (NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, Peshitta), Isa. 10:8 (i.e. this could refer to vassal kings)

- his (Tiglath-Pileser III, who reigned from 745-727 B.C., or possibly
Sennacherib, who reigned 705-681 B.C..) army has defeated several
other trans-Euphrates cities and nations, along with all their gods, Isa. 10:9

- Calno (or Calneh), city in northern Syria (cf. Amos 6:2) fell in
742 B.C. (all these dates are estimates only)

- Carchemish, major city of the Hittites near the headwaters of the Euphrates, joined
Assyrian coalition in 738 B.C.

- Hamath, city on the northern boundary of Israel (cf. 2 Chr. 8:4) on the Orontes River,
fell in 738 B.C.

- Arpad, city in northwest Syria fell in 741 B.C.

- Samaria (capital of Israel) fell in 722 B.C. to Sargon II

- Damascus (capital of Syria) fell in 732 B.C.

- he threatened to destroy Jerusalem and her "idols" as he had Samaria, Isa. 10:11. He had no
knowledge of the distinction between "idols" (cf. Isa. 2:8) and the true worship of YHWH.

Just a word about which Assyrian invasion is depicted. The place names follow a traditional
invasion route of ANE empires from Mesopotamia. Because of the desert, they had to follow the Euphrates
River to its headwaters and then go south along the coastal plain. The problem with identifying which
Assyrian invasion is complicated because Sennacherib, who did approach Jerusalem to besiege it, actually
came from the south of the city in 701 B.C. The fall of the cities mentioned
occurred under Tiglath-Pileser III (i.e. Pul). Therefore, I think the route was "idealized" as a
northern invader.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA

verses.zh: 迦勒挪岂不像迦基米施吗？哈马岂不像亚珥拔吗？撒马利亚岂不像大马士革吗？
verses.en: Is not Calneh like Carchemish?Hamath like Arpad?Samaria like Damascus?[NOTE:1]
notes: Calneh…Carchemish…Hamath…Arpad…Samaria…Damascus. The city states listed here were conquered by the Assyrians between 740-717 b.c. The point of the rhetorical questions is that no one can stand before Assyria’s might. On the geographical, rather than chronological arrangement of the cities, see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:264, n. 4.

verses.zh: 我手已经构到有偶像的国；这些国雕刻的偶像过于耶路撒冷和撒马利亚的偶像。
verses.en: I overpowered kingdoms ruled by idols,[NOTE:1] whose carved images were more impressive than Jerusalem’s[NOTE:2] or Samaria’s.
notes: Heb “Just as my hand found the kingdoms of the idol[s].” The comparison is expanded in v. 11a (note “as”) and completed in v. 11b (note “so”).
For the location of Jerusalem see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

verses.zh: 我怎样待撒马利亚和其中的偶像，岂不照样待耶路撒冷和其中的偶像吗？
verses.en: As I have done to Samaria and its idols,so I will do to Jerusalem and its idols.”[NOTE:1]
notes: The statement is constructed as a rhetorical question in the Hebrew text: “Is it not [true that] just as I have done to Samaria and its idols, so I will do to Jerusalem and its idols?’”sn This statement indicates that the prophecy dates sometime between 722-701 b.c.
verses.commentary:
10:11 "images" This is an interesting word (BDB 47). Its basic meaning is uncertain, but it is
spelled similarly to Elohim, which has caused scholars to assume it refers to weak and non-existent
idols (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 411). Monotheism is the uniqueness of Israel's
faith. There are other spiritual beings, but only one true God (cf. Deut. 4:35,39; 6:8; 32:39; Isa.
43:9-11; 45:21-22; Jer. 2:11; 5:7,10; Rom. 3:30; 1 Cor. 8:4,6; 1 Tim. 2:5; James 2:19). The idols
represent nothing, only the false hopes and fears (superstitions) of fallen humanity realizing there
is more to reality than the physical, but unable to comprehend spiritual truth (i.e. revelation).

Since vv. 8-11 refer to the arrogant claims of the Assyrian kings (as do vv. 13-14), v. 11 was
the invader's confidence that since his army had conquered many of the natives of Canaan and their gods (idols),
why should he not be able to do the same to Israel and Judah?

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

verses.zh: 主在锡安山和耶路撒冷成就他一切工作的时候，主说：「我必罚亚述王自大的心和他高傲眼目的荣耀。」
verses.en: But when[NOTE:1] the Lord[NOTE:2] finishes judging[NOTE:3] Mount Zion and Jerusalem, then he[NOTE:4] will punish the king of Assyria for what he has proudly planned and for the arrogant attitude he displays.[NOTE:5]
notes: The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here and in vv. 16, 23, 24, 33 is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay).
Heb “his work on/against.” Cf. NAB, NASB, NRSV “on”; NIV “against.”
Heb “I”; The Lord is speaking here, as in vv. 5-6a.

Heb “I will visit [judgment] on the fruit of the greatness of the heart of the king of Assyria, and on the glory of the height of his eyes.” The proud Assyrian king is likened to a large, beautiful fruit tree.
verses.commentary:
10:12-14 YHWH asserts His control of Assyria and her victories. He will judge the king of Assyria
(Isa. 10:12) for his

- arrogant heart

- haughtiness of his eyes (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP)

The Assyrian king's pride is shown in a series of self praises (Isa. 10:12-14), which sound
very much like Assyrian documents of the period (see The IVP Bible Background Commentary OT, p. 599)

- by the power of my hand

- by my wisdom

He robbed the nations on the west banks of the Euphrates as one robs a bird's nest!

verses.zh: 因为他说：我所成就的事是靠我手的能力和我的智慧，我本有聪明。我挪移列国的地界，抢夺他们所积蓄的财宝；并且我像勇士，使坐宝座的降为卑。
verses.en: For he says:“By my strong hand I have accomplished this,by my strategy that I devised.I invaded the territory of nations[NOTE:1] and looted their storehouses.Like a mighty conqueror,[NOTE:2] I brought down rulers.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “removed the borders of nations”; cf. NAB, NIV, NRSV “boundaries.”
The consonantal text (Kethib) has כְּאַבִּיר (keʾabbir, “like a strong one”); the marginal reading (Qere) is כַּבִיר (kavir, “mighty one”).

Heb “and I brought down, like a strong one, ones sitting [or “living”].” The participle יוֹשְׁבִים (yoshevim, “ones sitting”) could refer to the inhabitants of the nations, but the translation assumes that it refers to those who sit on thrones, i.e., rulers. See BDB 442 s.v. יָשַׁב and HALOT 444 s.v. ישׁב.
verses.commentary:
10:13

NASB
"like a mighty man"

NKJV
"like a valiant man"

NRSV, TEV, REB
"like a bull"

NJB
"like a hero"

The ADJECTIVE'S (BDB 7) basic meaning, "strong," can refer to

- mighty/violent man, Job 24:22; 34:20; Jer. 46:15; Lam. 1:15

- stubborn minded, Isa. 46:12

- angels, Ps. 78:25

- animals

- bulls, Isa. 10:13 may refer to a bull because a winged bull was the symbol of Assyria (i.e.
on the sides of the Ishtar gates, cf. Ps. 22:13; 68:30; Isa. 34:7)

- horses, Jdg. 5:22; Jer. 8:16; 47:3; 50:11

The ancient versions are very different in their understanding of this last poetic line of v. 13.

- LXX ‒ "and I will plunder their strength"

- Peshitta ‒ "and I have plundered their wealth, and subjugated the inhabited cities"

- the MT ‒ "I have brought down, like a bull, those who sat on thrones."

- JPSOA ‒ "I plundered their treasuries, and exiled their vast population."

verses.zh: 我的手构到列国的财宝，好像人构到鸟窝；我也得了全地，好像人拾起所弃的雀蛋。没有动翅膀的；没有张嘴的，也没有鸣叫的。
verses.en: My hand discovered the wealth of the nations, as if it were in a nest;as one gathers up abandoned eggs,I gathered up the whole earth.There was no wing flappingor open mouth chirping.”[NOTE:1]
notes: The Assyrians’ conquests were relatively unopposed, like robbing a bird’s nest of its eggs when the mother bird is absent.
verses.commentary:
10:14 The Bible often uses bird imagery to describe God's protection and care (cf. Exod. 19:4;
Deut. 32:11; Ruth 2:12; Isa. 31:5; Matt. 23:37; Luke 13:34; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADOW/SHADE),
but here the imagery is reversed! God has removed His protection!

The nations of the ANE were as defenseless as bird nests on the ground.

verses.zh: 斧岂可向用斧砍木的自夸呢？锯岂可向用锯的自大呢？好比棍抡起那举棍的，好比杖举起那非木的人。
verses.en: Does an ax exalt itself over the one who wields itor a saw magnify itself over the one who cuts with it?[NOTE:1] As if a scepter should brandish the one who raises itor a staff should lift up what is not made of wood!
notes: Heb “the one who pushes it back and forth”; KJV “him that shaketh it”; ASV “him that wieldeth it.”
verses.commentary:
10:15-19 YHWH responds to the boasts of the King of Assyria by questioning.

- Is the power in the axe or the one who used the axe?

- Is the power in the saw or the one who wields the saw?

- Is the power in the club or the one who swings the club?

- Is the power in a scepter or in the one who lifts the scepter?

YHWH will judge him and his army in one day (Isa. 10:17). This refers to

- Tiglath-Pileser III

- specifically to Sennacherib (701 B.C.), recorded in Isaiah 36-38;
2 Kgs. 18:17-21:11; 2 Chr. 32:9-24, where 185,000 soldiers die before the walls of Jerusalem in
response to the arrogance of the king of Assyria and his military leaders (#2 fits best, but
did not happen until decades after Tiglath-Pileser III took Samaria). There is a difference
between the God of Israel and the idols of the nations!

verses.zh: 因此，主―万军之耶和华必使亚述王的肥壮人变为瘦弱，在他的荣华之下必有火着起，如同焚烧一样。
verses.en: For this reason[NOTE:1] the Sovereign Lord of Heaven’s Armies will make his healthy ones emaciated.[NOTE:2] His majestic glory will go up in smoke.[NOTE:3]
notes: The irrational arrogance of the Assyrians (v. 15) will prompt the judgment about to be described.
Heb “will send leanness against his healthy ones”; NASB, NIV “will send a wasting disease.”

Heb “and in the place of his glory burning will burn, like the burning of fire.” The highly repetitive text (יֵקַד יְקֹד כִּיקוֹד אֵשׁ, yeqad yeqod kiqod’esh) may be dittographic; if the second consonantal sequence יקד is omitted, the text would read “and in the place of his glory, it will burn like the burning of fire.”
verses.commentary:
10:16 YHWH is in control of history. This is the basic premise of monotheism linked to an involved
Deity. He is present and active in His creation. In the OT all causality is attributed to YHWH (cf.
Deut. 32:29; Job 5:18; Isa. 45:7; Hosea 6:1; Amos 3:6; see SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY).
It was a way to affirm monotheism. Exactly how, when, where He acts is unknown, but there is

- an eternal redemptive plan (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)

- a covenant people (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT)

- a coming Messiah (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH)

- a heart for "the nations"

History is not cyclical, but teleological!

▣ "Lord" This is the Hebrew title Adon, which denoted "husband," "master," "owner." It is
parallel to the Greek title kurios.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

▣ "God of hosts" This is literally "YHWH of hosts" (BDB 217 and BDB 838).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "send a wasting disease" Diseases were common among large armies (cf. v. 18). See
IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 599.

▣ "His glory" See SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

▣ "fire" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

verses.zh: 以色列的光必如火；他的圣者必如火焰。在一日之间，将亚述王的荆棘和蒺藜焚烧净尽；
verses.en: The Light of Israel[NOTE:1] will become a fire,their Holy One[NOTE:2] will become a flame;it will burn and consume the Assyrian king’s[NOTE:3] briersand his thorns in one day.
notes: In this context the “Light of Israel” is a divine title (note the parallel title “Holy One”). The title points to God’s royal splendor, which overshadows and, when transformed into fire, destroys the “majestic glory” of the king of Assyria (v. 16b).
See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in 1:4.
Heb “his.” In vv. 17-19 the Assyrian king and his empire are compared to a great forest and orchard that are destroyed by fire (symbolic of the Lord).
verses.commentary:
10:17 "the light of Israel" This is a title for YHWH. Light (see note at Isa. 9:2) and fire are symbols of Deity
(cf. Isa. 9:19; 29:6; 30:27; 31:9; 33:11-12,14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIGHT

▣ "and His Holy One" This title is usually restricted to YHWH (cf. v. 20 and Isa. 37:23), but here, it
refers to the Messiah (or possibly the Death Angel, cf. 2 Kgs. 19:35; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE

Notice that the NASB translation thinks "his Holy One" refers to the "flame." Notice in line 2, the use
of the PRONOUN "it," but the PRONOUN "He" occurs again in v. 18.

verses.zh: 又将他树林和肥田的荣耀全然烧尽，好像拿军旗的昏过去一样。
verses.en: The splendor of his forest and his orchardwill be completely destroyed,[NOTE:1] as when a sick man’s life ebbs away.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “from breath to flesh it will destroy.” The expression “from breath to flesh” refers to the two basic components of a person, the immaterial (life’s breath) and the material (flesh). Here the phrase is used idiomatically to indicate totality.

The precise meaning of this line is uncertain. מָסַס (masas), which is used elsewhere of substances dissolving or melting, may here mean “waste away” or “despair.” נָסַס (nasas), which appears only here, may mean “be sick” or “stagger, despair.” See BDB 651 s.v. I נָסַס and HALOT 703 s.v. I נסס. One might translate the line literally, “like the wasting away of one who is sick” (cf. NRSV “as when an invalid wastes away”).
verses.commentary:
10:18-19 In these verses the Assyrian military is personified as trees in a forest (also note vv. 33-34).

Because of the mentioning "of his fruitful garden," these verses may also refer to the Assyrian
palaces (i.e. imagery for the nation).

10:18 "both soul and body" Mankind has both a physical component (i.e. nephesh; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH) and a spiritual component. We as humans are prepared for life on this
planet and for fellowship with a non-corporeal Deity! We share planet-life with animals, but we are also creatures of
the spiritual realm (cf. Gen. 1:26-27; Dan. 12:2)!

verses.zh: 他林中剩下的树必稀少，就是孩子也能写其数。
verses.en: There will be so few trees left in his forest,a child will be able to count them.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and the rest of the trees of his forest will be counted, and a child will record them.”
verses.commentary:
10:19 I have no idea what this line of poetry is referring to. The JPSOA translates this as "what trees remain of it
shrub, shall be so few that a boy may record them."

The Jewish Study Bible (Oxford) mentions that the remnant imagery used of God's faithful followers, is now
used of the defeated Assyrian army.

verses.zh: 到那日，以色列所剩下的和雅各家所逃脱的，不再倚靠那击打他们的，却要诚实倚靠耶和华―以色列的圣者。
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] those left in Israel, those who remain of the family[NOTE:2] of Jacob, will no longer rely on a foreign leader that abuses them.[NOTE:3] Instead they will truly[NOTE:4] rely on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “in that day.” The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
Heb “house” (so KJV, NASB, NIV84, NRSV).
Heb “on one who strikes him down.” This individual is the king (“foreign leader”) of the oppressing nation (which NLT specifies as “the Assyrians”).
Or “sincerely”; KJV, ASV, NAB, NRSV “in truth.”
See the note on the phrase “the Holy One of Israel” in 1:4.
verses.commentary:
10:20-23 This paragraph focuses on two theological truths.

- YHWH will protect and restore a faithful remnant ("truly rely on the Lord,"
BDB 1043, KB 1612, Niphal PERFECT with waw) to accomplish His purposes
with Abraham's seed.

- "In that day" refers to a day of deliverance. One is never sure if this promise is fulfilled in

- a return to Judah allowed by Persia (i.e. Cyrus II in 538 B.C.)

- the Maccabees (interbiblical period)

- the future time. The book that has really helped me understand the genre of Prophecy and Apocalyptic
is D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical
Prophecy and Apocalyptic.

10:20 "in that day" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

▣ "the remnant" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT, three senses

▣ "will never again rely on the one who struck them" Ahaz trusted/relied on Assyria for
help instead of YHWH, but not so in the future. The remnant (i.e. the covenant people) will rely on YHWH alone!

▣ "truly rely" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

▣ "the Holy One" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

verses.zh: 所剩下的，就是雅各家所剩下的，必归回全能的　神。
verses.en: A remnant will come back, a remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God.[NOTE:1]
notes: The referent of אֵל גִּבּוֹר (ʾel gibbor, “mighty God”) is uncertain. The title appears only here and in 9:6, where it is one of the royal titles of the coming ideal Davidic king. (Similar titles appear in Deut 10:17 and Neh 9:32 [“the great, mighty, and awesome God”] and in Jer 32:18 [“the great and mighty God”]. Both titles refer to God.) Though Hos 3:5 pictures Israel someday seeking “David their king,” and provides some support for a messianic interpretation of Isa 10:21, the Davidic king is not mentioned in the immediate context of Isa 10:21 (see Isa 11, however). The preceding verse mentions Israel relying on the Lord, so it is likely that the title refers to God here.
verses.commentary:
10:21 "A remnant will return" This remnant (BDB 984) is described as from Jacob and
Israel. In this context it must refer to the Northern Ten Tribes that split off in 922 B.C. and
were exiled by Assyria in 722 B.C. Few of them returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and
Joshua after Cyrus' edict in 538 B.C. allowed all the exiled people groups to return to their
native lands. The phrase translates Isaiah's first son's name (Shear-jashub) who went with his father to
confront King Ahaz (cf. Isa. 7:1-3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT, three senses

▣ "return" See SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣ "to the mighty God" This is the same title (i.e. El, BDB 42 plus the
ADJECTIVE "mighty" (BDB 150) used of the Messiah in Isa. 9:6. It is found only
in these two places. In this context it refers to YHWH.

verses.zh: 以色列啊，你的百姓虽多如海沙，惟有剩下的归回。原来灭绝的事已定，必有公义施行，如水涨溢。
verses.en: For though your people, Israel, are as numerous as[NOTE:1] the sand on the seashore, only a remnant will come back.[NOTE:2] Destruction has been decreed;[NOTE:3] just punishment[NOTE:4] is about to engulf you.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “are like.”

The twofold appearance of the statement “a remnant will come back” (שְׁאָר יָשׁוּב, sheʾar yashuv) in vv. 21-22 echoes and probably plays off the name of Isaiah’s son Shear Jashub (see 7:3). In its original context the name was meant to encourage Ahaz (see the note at 7:3), but here it has taken on new dimensions. In light of Ahaz’s failure and the judgment it brings down on the land, the name Shear Jashub now foreshadows the destiny of the nation. According to vv. 21-22, there is good news and bad news. The good news is that a remnant of God’s people will return; the bad news is that only a remnant will be preserved and come back. Like the name Immanuel, this name foreshadows both judgment (see the notes at 7:25 and 8:8) and ultimate restoration (see the note at 8:10).
Or “predetermined”; cf. ASV, NASB “is determined”; TEV “is in store.”
צְדָקָה (tsedaqah) often means “righteousness,” but here it refers to God’s just judgment.
Or “is about to overflow.”
verses.commentary:
10:22 "O Israel" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL

▣ "may be like the sand of the sea" This is a reference to the promise of many descendants, which
was a major part of the Abrahamic covenant (cf. Gen. 13:16; 22:17; 32:12).

What a sad contrast occurs when the promises of YHWH to the Patriarchs of many descendants (see
full note at Gen. 15:5).

- like the stars (cf. Gen. 15:5; 22:17; 26:4; Exod. 32:13; Deut. 1:10; 28:62)

- like the dust (cf. Gen. 13:16; 28:14)

- like the sand (cf. Gen. 22:17; 32:22)

is reduced through covenant disobedience and lack of personal trust (cf. Isa. 10:20) to only a
few to return (cf. Isa. 10:21-22).

▣ "A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness" Israel's judgment has been

- determined by YHWH, Isa. 10:22

- decreed by YHWH, Isa. 10:23

Both "determined" and "decreed" translate the same VERB (BDB 358,
KB 356, cf. Isa. 28:22; Dan. 9:26,27; 11:36). God will judge His people (Isa. 10:22). Isaiah 10:23 is (1) parallel
to this or (2) YHWH will judge all the earth (LXX, Peshitta, NRSV. Paul quotes the LXX in Rom. 9:27-28).
Context fits option #1 better. YHWH said He would do it; He did it!

verses.zh: 因为主―万军之耶和华在全地之中必成就所定规的结局。
verses.en: The Sovereign Lord of Heaven’s Armies is certainly ready to carry out the decreed destruction throughout the land.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “Indeed (or perhaps “for”) destruction and what is decreed the Sovereign Lord of Heaven’s Armies is about to accomplish in the middle of all the land.” The phrase כָלָא וְנֶחֱרָצָה (khalaʾ venekheratsah, “destruction and what is decreed”) is a hendiadys; the two terms express one idea, with the second qualifying the first.

verses.zh: 所以，主―万军之耶和华如此说：「住锡安我的百姓啊，亚述王虽然用棍击打你，又照埃及的样子举杖攻击你，你却不要怕他。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] here is what the Sovereign Lord of Heaven’s Armies says: “My people who live in Zion, do not be afraid of Assyria, even though they beat you with a club and lift their cudgel against you as Egypt did.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “therefore.” The message that follows is one of encouragement, for it focuses on the eventual destruction of the Assyrians. Consequently “therefore” relates back to vv. 5-21, not to vv. 22-23, which must be viewed as a brief parenthesis in an otherwise positive speech.
Heb “in the way [or “manner”] of Egypt.”
verses.commentary:
10:24-27 The paragraph again stresses YHWH's moral righteousness which is reflected in judgment
against evil.

- Israel experienced YHWH's righteous anger (cf. Isa. 10:22)

- Assyria (cf. Isa. 37:26-28)

- Like His wrath in Egypt during the Exodus (cf. Exod. 14:16,27)

- Like Gideon against the Midianites (Judges 6-8)

YHWH's actions, past and future, described in Isa. 10:27, are parallel to His action
(cf. Isa. 14:25) through the Messiah in Isa. 9:4, which also mentions the battle against Midian
(an idiom of YHWH's total defeat of an enemy cf. Isa. 9:4; Ps. 83:9-11).

10:24 "do not fear the Assyrian" This VERB (BDB 431, KB 432, Qal
IMPERFECT) is used as a JUSSIVE. The implication is "fear
YHWH who will bring judgment on them" (Isa. 10:25-27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

verses.zh: 因为还有一点点时候，向你们发的忿恨就要完毕，我的怒气要向他发作，使他灭亡。
verses.en: For very soon my fury[NOTE:1] will subside, and my anger will be directed toward their destruction.”
notes: The Hebrew text has simply “fury,” but the pronominal element can be assumed on the basis of what immediately follows (see “my anger” in the clause). It is possible that the suffixed yod (י) has been accidentally dropped by virtual haplography. Note that a vav (ו) is prefixed to the form that immediately follows; yod and vav are very similar in later script phases.

verses.zh: 万军之耶和华要兴起鞭来攻击他，好像在俄立磐石那里杀戮米甸人一样。耶和华的杖要向海伸出，把杖举起，像在埃及一样。
verses.en: The Lord of Heaven’s Armies is about to beat them[NOTE:1] with a whip, similar to the way he struck down Midian at the rock of Oreb.[NOTE:2] He will use his staff against the sea, lifting it up as he did in Egypt.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “him” (so KJV, ASV, NASB); the singular refers to the leader or king who stands for the entire nation. This is specified by NCV, CEV as “the Assyrians.”
According to Judg 7:25, the Ephraimites executed the Midianite general Oreb at a rock which was subsequently named after the executed enemy.

The Hebrew text reads literally, “and his staff [will be] against the sea, and he will lift it in the way [or “manner”] of Egypt.” One could emend the text of עַל הַיָּם (ʿal hayyam, “against the sea”) to עַלֵיהֶם (ʿalehem, “against them”). The proposed shift from the third singular pronoun (note “beat him” earlier in the verse) to the plural is not problematic, for the singular is collective. Note that a third plural pronoun is used at the end of v. 25 (“their destruction”). If the text is retained, as the translation does, “the sea” symbolizes Assyria’s hostility, the metaphor being introduced because of the reference to Egypt. The final phrase, “in the way/manner of Egypt,” probably refers to the way in which God used the staff of Moses to bring judgment down on Egypt.
verses.commentary:
10:26 "the rock of Oreb" Gideon summoned the Ephraimites to help him wipe out the remaining
retreating Midianites. Two of the leaders were caught and killed (cf. Jdg. 7:24-25). The place where
this occurred took on the names of the Midianite leaders, Oreb and Zeeb. The exact location is unknown.

▣ "His staff will be over the sea" As God delivered the Israelites at the Red Sea (Exodus), He
will deliver them from Assyria (here, called "the sea").

verses.zh: 到那日，亚述王的重担必离开你的肩头；他的轭必离开你的颈项；那轭也必因肥壮的缘故撑断（或译：因膏油的缘故毁坏）。」
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] the Lord will remove their burden from your shoulders[NOTE:2] and their yoke from your neck;the yoke will be taken off because your neck will be too large.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “in that day” (KJV). The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
Heb “he [i.e., the Lord] will remove his [i.e, Assyria’s] burden from upon your shoulder.”

The meaning of this line is uncertain. The Hebrew text reads literally, “and the yoke will be destroyed (or perhaps, “pulled down”) because of fatness.” Perhaps this is a bizarre picture of an ox growing so fat that it breaks the yoke around its neck or can no longer fit into its yoke. Fatness would symbolize the Lord’s restored blessings; the removal of the yoke would symbolize the cessation of Assyrian oppression. Because of the difficulty of the metaphor, many prefer to emend the text at this point. Some emend וְחֻבַּל (vekhubbal, “and it will be destroyed,” a perfect with prefixed vav), to יִחְבֹּל (yikhbol, “[it] will be destroyed,” an imperfect), and take the verb with what precedes, “and their yoke will be destroyed from your neck.” Proponents of this view (cf. NAB, NRSV) then emend עֹל (ʿol, “yoke”) to עָלָה (ʿalah, “he came up”) and understand this verb as introducing the following description of the Assyrian invasion (vv. 28-32). מִפְּנֵי שָׁמֶן (mippeney shamen, “because of fatness”) is then emended to read “from before Rimmon” (NAB, NRSV), “from before Samaria,” or “from before Jeshimon.” Although this line may present difficulties, it appears best to regard the line as a graphic depiction of God’s abundant blessings on his servant nation.
verses.commentary:
10:27

NASB, JPSOA
"the yoke will be broken because of fatness"

NKJV
"the yoke will be destroyed because of the

anointing oil"

LXX, REB
"the yoke will be destroyed from off your

shoulders"

Peshitta
"the yoke shall be destroyed from your neck

because of your strength"

NET
"the yoke will be taken off because

your neck will be too large"

From these translations you can see the options.

- NASB, JPSOA follow MT (the UBS Text Project, p. 35, gives this a "C" rating)

- LXX, REB leave out the phrase "because of fatness"

- NKJV refers to the Messiah (i.e. anointed, BDB 1032)

- Peshitta sees it as a reference to strength and growth (cf. Deut. 32:15), which may contrast Isa. 10:16.

- the NET Bible, p. 1205, #10, gives possible emendation

Since Isaiah 7-12 relates to the special children of the New Age, including the Messiah, I
like NKJV's understanding as the one that makes the most sense to me in this large literary unit, even though
this is not in the Hebrew root for Messiah, but it is a root used of "anointing."

The UBS Text Project, p. 26, says that the original Hebrew text may have contained
a place name.

- a place name which became an unknown place

- a proverbial location whose meaning is no longer recognized

- this links with place names in the next strophe

verses.zh: 亚述王来到亚叶，经过米矶仑，在密抹安放辎重。
verses.en: [NOTE:1] They[NOTE:2] attacked[NOTE:3] Aiath,moved through Migron,depositing their supplies at Micmash.
notes: Verses 28-31 display a staccato style; the statements are short and disconnected (no conjunctions appear in the Hebrew text). The translation to follow strives for a choppy style that reflects the mood of the speech.

Heb “he,” that is, the Assyrians (as the preceding context suggests). Cf. NCV “The army of Assyria.”sn Verses 28-32 describe an invasion of Judah from the north. There is no scholarly consensus on when this particular invasion took place, if at all. J. H. Hayes and S. A. Irvine (Isaiah, 209-10) suggest the text describes the Israelite-Syrian invasion of Judah (ca. 735 b.c.), but this proposal disregards the preceding context, which prophesies the destruction of Assyria. Some suggest that this invasion occurred in conjunction with Sargon’s western campaign of 713-711 b.c., but there is no historical evidence of such an invasion at that time. Many others identify the invasion as Sennacherib’s in 701 b.c., but historical records indicate Sennacherib approached Jerusalem from the southwest. J. N. Oswalt (Isaiah [NICOT], 1:274-75) prefers to see the description as rhetorical and as not corresponding to any particular historical event, but Hayes and Irvine argue that the precise geographical details militate against such a proposal. Perhaps it is best to label the account as rhetorical-prophetic. The prophecy of the invasion was not necessarily intended to be a literal itinerary of the Assyrians’ movements; rather its primary purpose was to create a foreboding mood. Geographical references contribute to this purpose, but they merely reflect how one would expect an Assyrian invasion to proceed, not necessarily how the actual invasion would progress. Despite its rhetorical nature, the prophecy does point to the invasion of 701 b.c., as the announcement of the invaders’ downfall in vv. 33-34 makes clear; it was essentially fulfilled at that time. For further discussion of the problem, see R. E. Clements, Isaiah (NCBC), 117-19. On the geographical details of the account, see Y. Aharoni, Land of the Bible, 393.
Heb “came against,” or “came to.”
verses.commentary:
10:28-32 H. C. Leupold, Exposition of Isaiah, vol. 1, p. 40, describes this stanza (strophe)
as "The Strategic Assyrian Advance That Almost Took Zion Described in Terms of Bulletin-from-the-Front."
Many geographical locations are mentioned and what was occurring at that location as the Assyrian mercenary
army approached.

10:28 "Aiath" This is Ai close to Jericho. The places mentioned show the movement of the Assyrians
toward Jerusalem from the north.

verses.zh: 他们过了隘口，在迦巴住宿。拉玛人战兢；扫罗的基比亚人逃跑。
verses.en: They went through the pass,spent the night at Geba.Ramah trembled,Gibeah of Saul ran away.

verses.zh: 迦琳的居民（原文是女子）哪，要高声呼喊！莱煞人哪，须听！哀哉！困苦的亚拿突啊。
verses.en: Shout out, daughter of Gallim!Pay attention, Laishah!Answer her, Anathoth![NOTE:1]
notes: The Hebrew text reads “Poor [is] Anathoth.” The parallelism is tighter if עֲנִיָּה (ʿaniyyah, “poor”) is emended to עֲנִיהָ (ʿaniha, “answer her”). Note how the preceding two lines have an imperative followed by a proper name.
verses.commentary:
10:30 "Cry aloud. . .Pay attention" These are both IMPERATIVES.

- BDB 843, KB 1007, Qal IMPERATIVE

- BDB 904, KB 1151, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

This breaks the pattern of Isa. 10:28-32. If this stanza is "reports from the front lines,"
then Isa. 10:30 is a comment from the prophet, not an Assyrian messenger.

NASB
"wretched Anathoth"

NKJV
"poor Anathoth"

NRSV, NET
"Answer her, O Anathoth"

TEV
"Answer, people of Anathoth"

NJB, REB, LXX
"Anathoth will listen"

Peshitta
"Answer me, O Anathoth"

JPSOA
"Take up the cry, Anathoth"

This is from either

- the VERB "answer," BDB 772 I, Qal IMPERATIVE (MT)

- an ADJECTIVE "poor," BDB 776

They both have the same CONSONANTS. UBS Hebrew Text Project gives #2, translated
"unfortunate,"a "C" rating (considerable doubt). It is surely possible that "poor" and "Anathoth"
are a sound play (NASB Study Bible, p. 974).

verses.zh: 玛得米那人躲避；基柄的居民逃遁。
verses.en: Madmenah flees,the residents of Gebim have hidden.

verses.zh: 当那日，亚述王要在挪伯歇兵，向锡安女子的山―就是耶路撒冷的山―抡手攻他。
verses.en: This very day, standing in Nob,they shake their fist at Daughter Zion’s mountain[NOTE:1]—at the hill of Jerusalem.
notes: The consonantal text (Kethib) has “a mountain of a house (בֵּית, bet), Zion,” but the marginal reading (Qere) correctly reads “the mountain of the daughter (בַּת, bat) of Zion.” On the phrase “Daughter Zion,” see the note on the same phrase in 1:8.
verses.commentary: 10:32 The second line of poetry expresses the Assyrian's contempt for Judah's God and His temple.

verses.zh: 看哪，主―万军之耶和华以惊吓削去树枝；长高的必被砍下，高大的必被伐倒。
verses.en: Look, the Sovereign Lord of Heaven’s Armiesis ready to cut off the branches with terrifying power.[NOTE:1] The tallest trees[NOTE:2] will be cut down,the loftiest ones will be brought low.
notes: The Hebrew text reads “with terrifying power,” or “with a crash.” מַעֲרָצָה (maʿaratsah, “terrifying power” or “crash”) occurs only here. Several have suggested an emendation to מַעֲצָד (maʿatsad, “ax”) parallel to “ax” in v. 34; see HALOT 615 s.v. מַעֲצָד and H. Wildberger, Isaiah, 1:448. sn As in vv. 12 (see the note there) and 18, the Assyrians are compared to a tree/forest in vv. 33-34.
Heb “the exalted of the height.” This could refer to the highest branches (cf. TEV) or the tallest trees (cf. NIV, NRSV).
verses.commentary:
10:33-34 Isa. 10:33-34 is hard to identify who is "lopped off." It seems to be a literary link
between Isa. 10:16-19 and 11:1. Isaiah often used forestry imagery. Whoever compiled the scroll of Isaiah
used word plays and themes as a way to link together Isaiah's recorded prophetic messages. We must remember
that the major truth of the literary unit and stanzas are more important than

- the details

- the exact historical setting of each literary building block

Our love for the Bible and desire to know more have caused us to treat the Bible in non-contextual,
literal ways, which destroy the literary nature of Scripture and especially Hebrew poetry and prophecy!

I think this is an elaboration of Isa. 10:16-19. The imagery is the destruction of a forest,
which symbolizes the Assyrian army and its leadership.

10:33 The second half of this verse has several terms found only here in the OT. This is why the
central truth of the paragraph (prose) or stanza (poetry) is crucial. The main truth or imagery is key,
not each and every detail or lexical option (often just an educated guess).

verses.zh: 稠密的树林，他要用铁器砍下；黎巴嫩的树木必被大能者伐倒。
verses.en: The thickets of the forest will be chopped down with an ax,and mighty Lebanon will fall.[NOTE:1]
notes: The Hebrew text has, “and Lebanon, by/as [?] a mighty one, will fall.” The translation above takes the preposition בְּ (bet) prefixed to “mighty one” as indicating identity, “Lebanon, as a mighty one, will fall.” In this case “mighty one” describes Lebanon. (In Ezek 17:23 and Zech 11:2 the adjective is used of Lebanon’s cedars.) Another option is to take the preposition as indicating agency and interpret “mighty one” as a divine title (see Isa 33:21). One could then translate, “and Lebanon will fall by [the agency of] the Mighty One.”

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject
divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the
original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ISAIAH 10:1-4

1Woe to those who enact evil statutes

And to those who constantly record unjust decisions,

2So as to deprive the needy of justice

And rob the poor of My people of their rights,

So that widows may be their spoil

And that they may plunder the orphans.

3Now what will you do in the day of punishment,

And in the devastation which will come from afar?

To whom will you flee for help?

And where will you leave your wealth?

4Nothing remains but to crouch among the captives

Or fall among the slain.

In spite of all this, His anger does not turn away

And His hand is still stretched out.
